title: Person-centred holistic assessment across the lifespan
blurb: Assess physical, psychological and social needs in partnership with the person, compare against their baseline and spot atypical presentations.
question: Mr Webb, 68, has a moderate learning disability and is admitted with abdominal pain. His support worker says he has become irritable and is refusing his favourite activities, which is unusual for him. How should the nurse interpret this?

teach.body: Holistic assessment gathers information about a person's physical, psychological, social and spiritual needs, and what matters to them, so that care fits their life rather than just their diagnosis. The NMC proficiencies ask you to apply knowledge of human development, body systems and the social and behavioural sciences (P3.1-3.3) and to take a person-centred approach with shared assessment, planning, decision making and goal setting (P3.4). In plain English: find out who this person is, what is normal for them, and what they want.
teach.cite: NMC Standards of proficiency (2018) P3.1-P3.4; Code 3, 2.1-2.3

teach.h: Four domains of a holistic assessment
teach.caption: Code 3: make sure people's physical, social and psychological needs are assessed and responded to.

teach.h: Start with what matters to the person
teach.body: A shared assessment begins by asking the person what matters most and what they hope to achieve, then building the clinical picture around it. Code 2.1-2.3: work in partnership, recognise the contribution people make to their own health, and empower them to share decisions. Code 1.3: avoid assumptions and recognise diversity and individual choice. Family and carers add vital detail, especially about the person's usual baseline.

teach.h: Atypical presentations to keep in mind
head: Who
What may be different
rows: Infection without fever; acute loss of function
Heart rate may not rise with infection
Illness may show as behaviour change or irritability
Lower baseline heart rate; normal BP doesn't exclude sepsis
teach.caption: NICE NG253 (2025) recs 1.4.1-1.4.10. Interpret mental state against the person's normal function.

teach.h: Scenario: Mr Webb and his support worker
teach.body: Mr Webb cannot easily describe his pain. His support worker knows him well and says irritability and refusing favourite activities are new. NICE NG253 notes that changes in cognitive function may show as behaviour change or irritability in adults with a learning disability, and that assessment should include history from family or carers. The nurse treats the change from his baseline as a possible sign of acute illness: full observations, NEWS2, an abdominal assessment, and escalation.

steps.label: History
steps.sub: From the person, then family or carers

steps.label: Compare to baseline
steps.sub: What is normal for THIS person?

teach.caption: Annexe B 1.2.2: recognise symptoms and signs of physical distress. NG31 recommends a validated behavioural pain tool for people who cannot report pain at the end of life.

items: Use age-appropriate tools and normal ranges: adult and children's early warning scores differ.
Ask about falls, continence, cognition, mood, vision, hearing and medicines in older people (NICE NG249).
Screen nutrition on admission (CG32) and assess pressure ulcer risk (CG179); check skin carefully in darker skin tones.
Identify and record communication needs and arrange support (Accessible Information Standard).

teach.text: Normal observations do not always mean a well patient. A frail 89-year-old with infection may have no fever; someone on bisoprolol may not become tachycardic. Look at the whole picture, including a change from baseline reported by people who know the person, and don't let a reassuring single number end the assessment.

items: Holistic: physical, psychological, social, spiritual and what matters to the person.
Shared assessment and goal setting with the person (P3.4; Code 2.1-2.3).
Use family and carers to establish baseline; change from baseline is significant.
Watch for atypical presentations: no fever in frail older people, blunted heart rate on beta-blockers, behaviour change in learning disability or dementia.
Recognise non-verbal signs of distress and pain (Annexe B 1.2.2).

summary: You can now carry out a person-centred assessment across physical, psychological, social and spiritual domains, use carers' knowledge of baseline, and recognise atypical and non-verbal presentations of illness and distress.

A.q: Mr Achebe, 62, is admitted with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes. The nurse wants the admission assessment to be person-centred and shared. Which opening is most appropriate?
options: Ask what matters most to him and what he hopes to achieve
Complete the trust checklist, then explain the plan to him
Ask his wife to describe his usual routine and difficulties
Review his medical notes and set targets for him to work on
A.why: P3.4: a person-centred approach with shared assessment, planning, decision-making and goal setting. Code 3.3 and 2.1: act in partnership with the person.

whyNot.1: Completing a checklist and then informing him is not shared assessment.
whyNot.2: His wife may add detail, but he can speak for himself and should be asked first.
whyNot.3: Setting targets for him rather than with him is not shared goal setting.

A.q: A nurse has completed a detailed physical assessment of Mr Rees, 75, admitted after a fall at home. Which further information is most important for a holistic assessment?
options: A repeat set of observations in four hours' time
A copy of his last outpatient clinic letter on file
His blood results from his previous hospital admission
His social circumstances, support and own priorities
A.why: Holistic assessment combines physical, psychological, social and spiritual needs with the person's goals (P3.1, P3.4; Code 3). After a fall at home, his living situation and support are central; NICE NG249 includes home hazard assessment.

whyNot.0: Repeat observations are routine but add no new domain to the assessment.
whyNot.1: Past letters add clinical history, not his current social needs.
whyNot.2: Old results add to the physical picture he already has.

A.q: Mrs Holt, 80, has advanced dementia and limited speech. During a wash she grimaces, guards her left hip and pulls away when it is touched. How should the nurse interpret these behaviours?
options: As part of her dementia that needs no further action
As resistance to care, so the wash should stop now
As non-verbal signs of distress that need assessment
As anxiety, so she should be offered reassurance
A.why: Annexe B 1.2.2: recognise signs of physical distress. Grimacing, guarding and withdrawal may indicate pain, so her hip needs further assessment (for example an injury from a fall).

whyNot.0: Attributing new signs to dementia risks missing pain or injury.
whyNot.1: Stopping the wash without assessing the hip misses the likely cause.
whyNot.3: Reassurance alone does not address possible pain or injury.

B.q: Mrs Fisher, 89, is frail and lives in a care home. She has become drowsy and less able to feed herself since yesterday. Her temperature is 36.8 °C. Her daughter is reassured she has no fever. What should the nurse explain?
options: A normal temperature makes infection unlikely at present
Her temperature should be checked again in 24 hours
The drowsiness is likely to be part of her normal ageing
Frail older people may have infection without a fever
B.why: NICE NG253 rec 1.4.1: do not rely on fever alone to rule sepsis in or out; rec 1.4.2: older or very frail people may not develop a raised temperature; rec 1.4.9: illness may present as acute change in function.

whyNot.0: Fever must not be relied on to rule out infection or sepsis.
whyNot.1: Waiting 24 hours delays assessment of an acute change.
whyNot.2: An acute change since yesterday is not normal ageing.

B.q: Mr Kim, 71, takes bisoprolol for heart failure. He has pneumonia, a respiratory rate of 24 and a heart rate of 74. A student says his normal pulse is reassuring. What is the best response?
options: Agree, as a pulse under 90 suggests he is not septic
Explain beta-blockers can blunt a rise in heart rate
Agree, as his NEWS2 score will be within normal limits
Explain heart rate is not used in assessing older people
B.why: NICE NG253 rec 1.4.4: interpret heart rate in context; older people may not develop a raised heart rate, and it may be affected by beta-blockers. His raised respiratory rate still needs scoring and escalation.

whyNot.0: A normal pulse does not exclude sepsis, especially on beta-blockers.
whyNot.2: RR 24 scores 2 on NEWS2, so his score is not zero, and a single parameter can mislead.
whyNot.3: Heart rate is assessed in all adults, but interpreted in context.

B.q: Mrs Patel, 58, is two days after bowel surgery. Her NEWS2 is 4. The nurse notices her knees are mottled and her lips look slightly blue. How should this change the nurse's assessment?
options: She may be at higher risk than her NEWS2 suggests
It suggests she is cold and needs extra blankets
It does not alter care, as the NEWS2 score is below 5
It should be recorded and reviewed at the next round
B.why: NICE NG253 rec 1.6.3: consider a higher risk of severe illness or death from sepsis than NEWS2 suggests if there is a mottled or ashen appearance or cyanosis. These signs of physical ill health (Annexe B 1.2.1) need urgent escalation.

whyNot.1: Mottling and cyanosis after surgery need assessment for sepsis, not just warming.
whyNot.2: Clinical signs can indicate greater risk than the score shows.
whyNot.3: Waiting for a round delays urgent assessment.

C.q: Mr Webb, 68, has a moderate learning disability and abdominal pain. His support worker says he has become irritable and refuses his favourite activities, which is unusual. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: As behaviour linked to his known learning disability
As a reaction to the unfamiliar hospital environment
As a reason to ask for a positive behaviour support plan
As a possible sign of acute illness needing assessment
C.why: NICE NG253 rec 1.4.8: changes in cognitive function may present as behaviour change or irritability in adults with a learning disability; rec 1.4.7: include history from family or carers. A change from baseline is significant.

whyNot.0: Attributing new behaviour to his learning disability is diagnostic overshadowing and may miss illness.
whyNot.1: The change began before admission and is reported as new for him.
whyNot.2: Behaviour support is not the first response to an acute change with abdominal pain.

C.q: Mr Ortiz, 66, is profoundly deaf and uses British Sign Language. He is being admitted for elective surgery in England. What does the Accessible Information Standard require?
options: Identify, record, flag and meet his needs with a BSL interpreter
Provide written information so he can read about his surgery in advance
Ask his hearing partner to interpret at the admission assessment
Speak slowly and clearly so he can lip-read during the assessment
C.why: The Accessible Information Standard (DAPB1605, updated June 2025) requires services to identify, record, flag, share and meet communication needs; for a BSL user this means a qualified interpreter (Code 7.2).

whyNot.1: Written English may not be accessible to a BSL user and does not meet the standard.
whyNot.2: A family member is not a professional interpreter and may not convey information accurately.
whyNot.3: Lip-reading is unreliable and does not meet his recorded communication need.

C.q: A nurse is assessing Mrs Grace, 79, who has fallen twice this year. Which approach best reflects current NICE falls guidance?
options: Use a falls risk prediction tool to decide whether to assess her
Offer a comprehensive assessment including medicines and vision
Advise her to stay in bed until a physiotherapist has seen her
Refer her to the GP once she has had a third fall this year
C.why: NICE NG249 (2025): do not use falls risk prediction tools; offer comprehensive falls assessment (including medicines review, vision, gait, continence, cognition) to people who have fallen and meet the criteria, such as 2 or more falls in a year.

whyNot.0: NG249 says do not use falls risk prediction tools to predict risk.
whyNot.2: Bed rest causes deconditioning and is not part of assessment.
whyNot.3: Two falls in a year already meet the criteria for assessment.

reteach.title: Ask: what's normal for this person, and what's changed?
reteach.question: If you could only ask two questions about a new patient, which would reveal the most?

blocks.body: Every assessment is a comparison. The same heart rate, temperature or behaviour can be normal for one person and alarming for another. So ask the person, and the people who know them, what their usual self is like: mobility, mood, appetite, behaviour, abilities. Then look for change. New irritability in someone with a learning disability, new confusion in an older person, or sudden loss of function can be the first sign of serious illness.

blocks.text: Diagnostic overshadowing: blaming a new sign on an existing condition (dementia, learning disability) and missing the real illness.

explain.body: Physical, psychological, social and spiritual or cultural needs, plus what matters to the person (Code 3; P3.1-3.4).

test.q: Which finding belongs to the social domain of a holistic assessment?
options: He cares for his wife who has dementia
His mood has been low for two weeks
He has a sacral pressure ulcer
He wishes to see the hospital chaplain
test.why: Caring responsibilities are social circumstances that affect discharge planning and support needs.

whyNot.1: Mood belongs to the psychological domain.
whyNot.2: A pressure ulcer is a physical finding.

explain.body: Start with the person's priorities; share assessment, planning and goal setting (P3.4); avoid assumptions (Code 1.3); involve family and carers, especially to establish baseline.

test.q: Which statement best reflects shared goal setting?
options: "We've decided you'll walk to the toilet by Friday."
"Your consultant wants you home by the weekend."
"What would you most like to be able to do again?"
"Most patients manage the stairs by day five."
test.why: An open question about the person's own goals starts shared goal setting (P3.4; Code 2.3).

whyNot.0: This goal has been set for the person, not with them.
whyNot.1: This reflects the team's goal, not the person's.
whyNot.3: Comparing with typical patients is not person-centred.

explain.body: No fever in older or frail people; blunted heart rate on beta-blockers; illness showing as behaviour change in learning disability or dementia; pulse oximeters may overestimate SpO2 in darker skin (NICE NG253).

test.q: Why should a nurse interpret a pulse oximeter reading with caution in a patient with dark skin?
options: Readings may underestimate oxygen levels
Readings may overestimate oxygen levels
The probe cannot detect a pulse reliably
Readings take longer to stabilise
test.why: NICE NG253 notes that overestimation of oxygen saturation has been reported in people with dark skin, which could hide hypoxia.

whyNot.0: The reported problem is overestimation, which can mask low oxygen.
whyNot.2: Pulse detection is not the issue described.
whyNot.3: Stabilisation time is not the concern NICE describes.

explain.body: Grimacing, guarding, withdrawal, agitation or sudden loss of abilities may signal pain or illness in people who cannot report it (Annexe B 1.2.2). Compare with baseline and assess the cause.

test.q: A man with dementia who is usually calm has become agitated and keeps rubbing his abdomen. What should the nurse do first?
options: Ask for a sedative to settle him
Document it as dementia progression
Increase the level of observation
Assess him for pain and its cause
test.why: A change from baseline with a body cue suggests pain or illness; assess it first (Annexe B 1.2.2).

whyNot.0: Sedation does not address the cause and may be chemical restraint.
whyNot.1: This is diagnostic overshadowing and may miss serious illness.
whyNot.2: Observation does not identify or treat the cause.
